327	## Migration safety concerns
328	
329	The S1 validation query is wrong for OOB. §16.1 says `artifact_topics` count equals memories + themes + observations + watch_items + distillations + out_of_bounds (§16.1, lines 614–615), but S3 says global OOB is represented by no `artifact_topics` rows (§16.3, line 695). If existing OOB rows are all backfilled with topic rows, you have silently made them non-global. If they are not backfilled, the validation fails. This needs an explicit classification/backfill rule before S1.
330	
331	The S1 artifact backfill is safer than a table rewrite, but still not “just additive.” Existing artifact tables have useful per-table indexes [0001_init.sql](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/Veas/migrations/0001_init.sql:155), and distillations add several GIN indexes [0015_distillations.sql](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/Veas/migrations/0015_distillations.sql:57). A large `artifact_topics` backfill creates a new write-amplified table and two partial indexes. Batched `UPDATE ... LIMIT 5000` is not the right shape for a pure join-table insert; use id-range or cursor-keyed `INSERT INTO artifact_topics SELECT ... WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n`, with resumability and duplicate protection. Also: the design join table has no real FK to each artifact table, so orphan prevention is entirely application discipline.
332	
333	The S2 `NOT NULL` flip needs a rollback rule. Once `messages.bot_id/topic_id` and `bot_turns.bot_id/topic_id` are NOT NULL (§16.2, line 656), rolling back to the old app code will break inserts immediately. The plan needs a deploy gate: after NOT NULL, old app versions are no longer valid rollback targets. Safer is add `CHECK (bot_id IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, validate, then set NOT NULL only after the new code has survived a full rollback window.
334	
335	The byte-identical DoD is unrealistic. Hot context embeds current timestamps [hot_context.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/Veas/app/services/hot_context.py:65), relative temporal labels [time_context.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/Veas/app/services/time_context.py:98), and rendered current-time blocks [hot_context.py](/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/Veas/app/services/hot_context.py:592). A realistic check is deterministic fixture rendering with frozen `now`, fixed DB snapshot, and normalized IDs/timestamps, plus production semantic diff on section counts/order, not prompt hash equality between real turns.
336	
337	## What's missing entirely
338	
339	Per-sprint rollback procedures are missing. S1 needs “remove code, keep additive schema” guidance. S2 needs a hard no-rollback-after-NOT-NULL statement. S3 needs a read-path feature flag to bypass joins if latency spikes. S4 needs a way to disable `scope` exposure without disabling enforcement. S5 needs a kill switch for the solo bot by `bot_id/channel_id`.
340	
341	Production observability is underdeveloped until S6 (§16.6, line 830), which is too late. S2 should already log `bot_id`, `topic_id`, `channel_id`, `binding_id` on inbound, turns, outbound, scheduled jobs, and OOB checks. S5 should not be the first time dashboards can split mediator vs solo.
342	
343	The solo bot pre-flight should move to S4: bot account/phone provisioning, webhook endpoint/channel records, secrets, provider allowlists, transport-specific OOB tests, and a consenting target user with written expectations. §16.5 names provisioning lead time (§16.5, line 771), but leaves it in the riskiest sprint.
344	
345	You also need an eval baseline before S3/S4, not S6. The plan defers per-bot eval scaffolding to S6 (§16.6, line 831), but mediator regressions from tool-schema changes and prompt context changes are exactly what S3/S4 can cause.
346	
347	## Highest-risk single moment in the plan
348	
349	The riskiest moment is S2 day 8–9: after routing is wired, hot-path inserts are stamped, in-memory coalescing and newer-inbound suppression are rekeyed, scheduled jobs start carrying bot identity, artifact writes become multi-row transactions, and then `NOT NULL` is applied (§16.2, lines 648–656). That single deploy window can break live replies, create duplicate/stale replies, orphan artifacts, or make rollback impossible. Split S2 into “stamp/rekey with nullable columns” and “constraints after soak,” or extend it.

> AGENT

Sharp review. Verdict: **not shippable as written.** Real defects across S2, S3, S4, and S5. Concrete summary:

## Findings that matter

**S2 is genuinely too large.** Combines insert-site stamping + coalescer rekey + newer-inbound rekey + scheduled-job bot routing + artifact-write transactions + NOT NULL in a 10-workday sprint with a 7-day soak. No margin to find a missed insert and restart the soak. The list of insert sites I had was incomplete — also `agentic.py:577` (deferred jobs), `scheduled_jobs.py:216` (scheduler seeds), `write_tools.py:1367` (scheduled-task writes).

**S3 is a full data-access audit, not a query helper refactor.** Hot context reads all six artifact families at multiple sites; `scheduled_job_handlers.py:243` counts themes/watch items; `decay.py:41` mutates global themes/observations/watch items without any topic restriction (won't survive multi-bot). 30–50 was an underestimate.

**S4 has 19 read-phase tools** plus read surfaces hiding in `write_tools.py` (e.g. `list_scheduled_tasks`). Adding `scope` to every one changes model-visible schemas — a behavior-risk sprint, not plumbing.

**S5 under-scopes everything that isn't code.** Transport provisioning, webhook setup, secrets, channel registration, consent, transport-specific OOB testing — all sit in the riskiest sprint instead of being pre-flighted in S4.

## Three concrete defects, not just sizing

1. **OOB backfill rule is ambiguous.** S1 validation says counts equal sum-of-rows; S3 says global OOB is "no `artifact_topics` rows." So either existing OOB rows become topic-scoped (silently lose globality) or they don't (validation fails). Needs an explicit rule: **existing OOB backfills to `relationship` topic** (not global). Global is a new mode introduced for the future.

2. **`consult_perspective` doesn't clone — it reconstructs.** `consult_perspective.py:105` builds a fresh `TurnContext` field-by-field. Every new field added in S1 is dropped on entry unless the constructor is updated. The S4 line "clone ctx preserving scopes" is wrong; the work item should be "replace manual constructor with a dataclass clone helper and test all fields."

3. **Byte-identical DoD is unrealistic.** Hot context embeds `now_utc`, relative time labels, current-time blocks (`hot_context.py:65, 592`). Equal hashes between live turns is impossible. Should be: frozen-fixture rendering equality (deterministic snapshot, frozen `now`, normalized ids) + production semantic diff on section counts/order.

## What's missing entirely

- **Per-sprint rollback procedures.** Especially S2: once NOT NULL applies, old app versions can't be rolled back to. Safer pattern: `CHECK ... NOT VALID` → VALIDATE → NOT NULL after the new code has survived a full rollback window.
- **Observability before S6.** Per-bot logging on inbound/turns/outbound/jobs/OOB needs to land in S2 alongside the stamping work, not in S6.
- **Eval baseline before S3/S4.** Tool-schema and prompt changes in those sprints are exactly what regress the mediator. Snapshot evals before S3.
- **Pause depth.** `system_state.is_paused` is global; per-(user, bot) pause needs at least partial bringup in S2 since the coalescer and scheduler are already being rekeyed.

## Proposed delta to §16

**Split S2 into S2a and S2b. Plan becomes 7 sprints.**

- **S2a (Stamp + rekey, nullable).** Routing wired into inbound. All insert sites stamp `bot_id`/`topic_id`/`channel_id`. Coalescer + newer-inbound suppression rekeyed with a dual-key transitional version (`(user_id, bot_id)` AND legacy `user_id` keys both serviced for one deploy). Per-bot observability bringup. Eval baseline captured. Partial per-(user, bot) pause bringup. **No NOT NULL.**
- **S2b (Constraints + rollback gate).** Soak for 7 days. `CHECK ... NOT VALID` then VALIDATE then NOT NULL. Drop legacy keys from dual-key code paths. Tests/fixtures finalized.

**S4 absorbs solo bot pre-flight as parallel work.** Transport provisioning, webhook/channel records, secrets, consent, transport-specific OOB tests get done in S4 so S5 is purely the code work.

**Three pointed fixes:**

- §16.1 work item: explicit OOB classification on backfill — all existing OOB → `relationship` topic-scoped. Validation query updated.
- §16.1 work item: cursor-keyed `INSERT INTO artifact_topics SELECT ... WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n` with resumability, not batched UPDATE.
- §16.4 work item: `consult_perspective` rewritten with a shared dataclass-clone helper (e.g. `dataclasses.replace(ctx, …)`) and a unit test that enumerates every `TurnContext` field. Lint that asserts the test enumerates them all.

**Add to every sprint:** explicit rollback procedure subsection.

**Move per-bot eval scaffolding from S6 to S2a.** Baseline pre-S3.

---

The full review will go in as §21 (verification record). Do you want me to apply the §16 deltas — split S2, move pre-flight/observability/evals, fix the three concrete defects — and we end up with a 7-sprint plan that's actually shippable? Or push back on any of the calls?

**Sprint table:**

| # | Title |
|---|---|
| 1 | Foundation schema + code shape |
| **2a** | **Stamp + rekey (nullable), observability, eval baseline** |
| **2b** | **Constraints + soak gate** |
| 3 | `artifact_topics` join cutover |
| 4 | Authorization + topic status + **solo pre-flight** |
| 5 | First solo bot (code only) |
| 6 | Multi-topic writes + hardening |

**Concrete defects fixed:**

- **OOB backfill rule** (§16.1): existing OOB rows all → `relationship` topic-scoped. "No `artifact_topics` rows = global OOB" is a future-only mode, no current rows use it. Validation query updated.
- **Backfill mechanism** (§16.1): cursor-keyed `INSERT INTO artifact_topics SELECT ... WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n` with resumability via a `migration_progress` table — not batched UPDATEs.
- **Byte-identical DoD** (§16.1): frozen-fixture rendering equality + production semantic diff on section counts/order/ids. Live `prompt_snapshot` hash equality is impossible because hot context embeds `now_utc` and relative time labels.
- **`consult_perspective` clone** (§16.5, work item 2): replace the field-by-field `TurnContext` reconstruction at `consult_perspective.py:105` with a `dataclasses.replace` helper. Enumeration unit test + lint that fails on any new `TurnContext(...)` constructor outside the helper.
- **`decay.py` per-topic decision** (§16.4, work item 3): explicit decision required — recommend per-topic. Documented and property-tested.
- **`agentic.py:686` partner_of fix** (§16.6, work item 6): runner skips partner resolution when `participants_shape == "solo"`. Single line that breaks solo support today.

**Bigger-picture changes:**

- **Dual-key transition** (§16.2): coalescer + newer-inbound suppression service both `(user_id)` and `(user_id, bot_id)` keys during S2a; legacy paths retired in S2b.
- **`CHECK ... NOT VALID` → VALIDATE → NOT NULL** pattern (§16.3): rollback-safe constraint application.
- **Observability + eval baseline moved to S2a** (work items 6, 8). Without them, S3 and S4 can't detect regressions.
- **Solo pre-flight moved to S4** (§16.5, work items 10–15): transport provisioning, webhook config, secrets, OOB transport tests, consent, staging-only `bots`/`channels` rows. S5 becomes pure code work.
- **Per-(user, bot) pause split**: read-path in S2a (so coalescer/scheduler can consult it during rekey), write-path admin endpoint in S4.

   - Dual-key transitional cutover for coalescer/suppression rekey

# Profile selection — picking models per phase, with thinking-strength tiers

> **Living document.** Refine after every meaningful bake-off — the entries below should keep shrinking and sharpening, not growing.

Three dials, picked independently each time you reach for megaplan:

- **Profile** — which model handles which phase.
- **Thinking strength** — how hard each model thinks.
- **Robustness** — which phases actually run and how many critique checks happen.

Default to the cheapest tier of each dial that still produces correct output. When in doubt, pick the next tier up — one tier of money is bounded, but undershooting can mean a re-run, an undetected bug, or a hallucinated decision that propagates downstream. **Pay for what the *artifact* is, not how long the work takes** — a 2-week sprint of mechanical scripts is fine on a low tier; a 3-day sprint defining a permanent schema is what the apex is for.

## Set up as a Claude / Codex skill

This doc doubles as the SKILL.md body for the `megaplan-model-selection` skill. To wire it up so Claude Code and Codex consult it automatically when picking a profile, symlink this file into the skill dirs — symlinking (rather than copying) keeps the canonical doc here in the megaplan repo and avoids drift:

```bash
DOC="$(pwd)/docs/profile-selection.md"   # run from the megaplan repo root

# Claude Code skill
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/megaplan-model-selection
ln -sf "$DOC" ~/.claude/skills/megaplan-model-selection/SKILL.md

# Codex skill
mkdir -p ~/.codex/skills/megaplan-model-selection
ln -sf "$DOC" ~/.codex/skills/megaplan-model-selection/SKILL.md
```

Restart Claude Code / Codex after symlinking so they pick up the new skill. Edits to this file propagate to both skills automatically. If multiple people on a team want the skill, each runs the same commands against their own local checkout — never share a symlink to someone else's path.

The "detective cluster" profiles listed below (`marlowe-*`, `spade-*`, `holmes-*`, `watson-*`) plus the standalone profiles (`nancy`, `all-claude`, `poirot`) are shipped as built-ins in `megaplan/profiles/`, so `megaplan run --profile <name>` resolves out of the box once megaplan is installed. Project-local overrides go in `<project>/.megaplan/profiles.toml`; per-user overrides in `~/.config/megaplan/profiles.toml`.

## The profiles

Each profile has a practical name, a detective-personality moniker, and a dash-shorthand showing which model handles which phase. For any profile with both `-claude` and `-codex` variants, pick the variant by user preference, available credits, or which model has done better on similar work in this codebase.

### The standalone profiles

| Profile | Models per phase | Cost band (per phase, light) | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`nancy`** *(Nancy Drew — sharp-eyed light-touch detective)* | DeepSeek plan/revise/finalize/execute — codex:medium prep/critique/gate/review | ~-3 | Verification, smoke tests, runbook authoring, doc-mode plans, anything mostly text. Cheapest viable profile. |
| **`all-claude`** *(Adrian Monk — solo virtuoso obsessed with thoroughness)* / **`all-codex`** *(Lt. Columbo — solo analyst, "just one more thing")* | Opus 4.7 / GPT-5.5 default-effort — every phase | ~-70 | Kernel-invariant changes, contract definition (a selector schema, a wire format), anything where regression = production incident. Pair with `--robustness robust` for extremely complex projects. |
| **`poirot`** *(Hercule Poirot — methodical, combines deduction with observation)* | Claude plan/prep/revise/gate/finalize — codex critique/execute/review | ~-50 | **Apex tier.** Both premiums contributing simultaneously, leveraged for their strengths (Claude on author/gate side, codex on critique/execute side). Reach for this when a single-model premium isn't enough — multi-system migration decisions, high-stakes contract definition with downstream cascades. |

### The detective cluster — an 8-profile grid

The bread-and-butter middle tier. All cells share the same mechanical floor (DeepSeek V4 Pro handles `prep` / `finalize` / `execute`); they differ only on the **reasoning** phases (`plan` / `critique` / `revise` / `gate` / `review`).

Three independent axes determine the cell:

1. **Effort tier (row)** — low (marlowe/spade) vs medium (holmes/watson). Match the stakes: low for routine implementation, medium for novel code or wider blast radius.
2. **Critic strategy (column)** — premium-mono (critic = author) vs Kimi K2.6 (cheap sidekick). Default to Kimi; upgrade to premium-mono when the critic needs to catch deep structural flaws Kimi might miss.
3. **Author model (variant within each cell)** — Claude (Opus 4.7) vs Codex (GPT-5.5). Pick by user preference, credits, or prior fit on similar work in this codebase.

| | **Premium-mono critic** *(critic = author)* | **Kimi K2.6 critic** *(cheap sidekick)* |
|---|---|---|
| **Low effort** *(routine implementation)* | **`marlowe-claude`** / **`marlowe-codex`** *(Philip Marlowe — hard-boiled gumshoe, gets the job done day after day)* ~-15 | **`spade-claude`** / **`spade-codex`** *(Sam Spade — gumshoe with a partner, here the partner is Kimi)* ~-5 |
| **Medium effort** *(belt-and-braces)* | **`holmes-claude`** / **`holmes-codex`** *(Sherlock Holmes — meticulous master, leaves nothing to chance)* ~-30 | **`watson-claude`** / **`watson-codex`** *(Dr. Watson — Holmes's affordable companion, Kimi plays the supporting role)* ~-25 |

### Legacy profile names

- **`marlowe`** (legacy) is functionally identical to **`spade-claude`** — same models, kept as an alias so existing scripts keep working. Either name resolves.
- **`holmes`** (legacy) is *not* identical to `watson-claude`: it has a cross-model gate (`codex:medium` gate/review while `claude:medium` plans/revises), pairing Opus authoring depth with codex's analytical post-iteration check. Kept as a distinct profile for medium-stakes work where the cross-model gate is the point.

## Pick by deliverable type

A profile is chosen per **sprint** — and a sprint is at most ~2 weeks of work. So you're really picking a profile for "this 2-week chunk." Triage by the shape of the chunk's deliverable. Stakes-level questions (downstream cascades? security? production-incident blast radius?) override the table — if any of those applies, jump to the apex row.

| Project shape | Cluster row / profile | Robustness | Example deliverables |
|---|---|---|---|
| Discovery, snapshot, smoke tests, runbook, docs | `nancy` | `light` | Pre-sprint codebase snapshot, dependency inventory, SKILL.md / AGENTS.md rewrite, regression-workload setup. |
| Mechanical migration, well-shaped utility, port of simple existing code, legacy-surface deletion | Low-effort row (marlowe/spade) | `light` (use `standard` if the change touches many files) | Schema-to-schema migrations, fixture corpus, inventory script, hash-chain reader, cost rollups, dead-YAML removal, port of a self-contained utility. |
| Cross-cutting feature work, novel code in a known architecture, plumbing rewrites with edge cases, CRUD over a new schema, ports needing judgment | Medium-effort row (holmes/watson — prefer `-claude` when porting existing code, since Opus reads existing repos better as a planner) | `standard` | New CLI gate + status rewrite, inbox routing rewrite, adapters in a known shape, plan-mutation verbs, timeline/project export surfaces. |
| **Apex:** high-stakes work or big architectural decisions | `poirot` (default — both premiums on one job) or `all-claude` / `all-codex` for a single-model pipeline | `robust` | Concurrency primitives (lease + locked event-append + writer epoch + session schema), schemas later sprints all depend on (step schema + plan replay + supersession; timeline manifest), remote-artifact adapters that downstream code assumes, security work, kernel-invariant changes. |

**The apex row is where dual-premium `poirot` belongs.** Reach for it when *either* condition is true:

1. **High stakes** — security, data migrations, kernel-invariant changes, public API contracts, anything where a regression = production incident.
2. **Big architectural decisions** — the sprint *makes* the decision (concurrency model, schema, wire format, claim semantics) rather than just implementing one already made. Downstream sprints will all depend on what you decide here.

Default to `poirot` over `all-claude` / `all-codex` for the apex tier — `poirot` gets you both Claude and codex perspectives in one job rather than two parallel runs. Choose `all-claude` (robust) instead when one model definitively reads or writes this specific area better — e.g., a schema that sits over an existing rich data structure favors `all-claude` because Opus reads existing code better as a planner. For apex picks, also bump the plan phase via `--phase-model plan=claude:high` (or `plan=codex:high` for poirot's codex-author side) — the planner-high / critic-low asymmetry beats `claude:medium` everywhere on cost and matches it on quality.

**One thing that overrides the table:** if a single sprint mixes deliverable types (code patches AND runbook updates AND ops dashboards), split it into separate megaplan jobs by work type. Don't pay premium for the runbook just because the same sprint also has a contract change.

## Thinking strength

Both Claude and Codex accept a thinking-strength tier that's independent of the model. It's spelled out in the agent spec after a colon:

- Claude: `claude:low`, `claude:medium`, `claude:high`, `claude:xhigh`, `claude:max`.
- Codex: `codex:minimal`, `codex:low`, `codex:medium`, `codex:high`.

The principle: **author-side phases (plan, revise) reward higher thinking strength; sense-check phases (prep, critique, gate, review) plateau at low or medium.**

| Phase | Recommended strength | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **plan** | medium-to-high | Authoring is where thinking earns its keep. Bump to `high` when the codebase is unfamiliar or the brief is long. Stay at `medium` for routine work. Use `xhigh` / `max` only for genuinely novel architectural plans. |
| **revise** | medium-to-high | Same as plan — author-side. Pair with whatever you used for plan. |
| **critique** | low-to-medium | Critique is recognition, not generation. `low` is usually enough; `medium` if you suspect deep structural issues. |
| **gate** | low | Single iterate/proceed decision from existing artifacts. The experiment showed `claude:low` and `claude` default produced identical gate verdicts on the same plans. |
| **review** | low | Same logic as gate. |
| **prep** | low | Repository inspection. |
| **finalize / execute** | minimal-to-low | Mechanical translation from plan to tasks, then mechanical task execution. Don't pay for thinking here. |

The general rule: a **`claude:high` planner with a `claude:low` critic is the right asymmetry**, not `claude:medium` everywhere. Same for codex.

You usually don't need a separate profile per tier — pass `--phase-model plan=claude:high` on the CLI to bump just the authoring tier on top of an existing profile. Reserve named profile variants for tiers you reach for repeatedly.

## Robustness

Set with `--robustness <level>` on the megaplan command.

| Level | Workflow | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| (skip megaplan) | — | Single-file fixes, trivial changes, anything you can hold in your head. Just do the work directly. |
| `light` | plan → critique → revise → finalize → execute. No prep, no gate, no review. | Small/scoped changes, well-known features, low blast radius. ~5 phases instead of 8. Cheap and fast. |
| `standard` *(default)* | prep → plan → critique → gate → revise → finalize → execute → review. 4 critique checks. | Default for any work that's not narrowly scoped. Cross-cutting changes, unfamiliar code, ambiguous requirements. |
| `robust` | Same shape as standard but 8 critique checks (vs 4) and parallel critique. | High-stakes: security, data migrations, public API changes, contracts the rest of the system depends on. The plan itself needs rigorous debate. |
| `superrobust` | robust + parallel review. | Rarely needed. Use when both deep critique and concurrent review matter and you can absorb the parallelism cost. |

Cost bands in the profile tables above are at `light`. Expect roughly 1.5-2× the per-phase cost going from light → standard, and another ~1.3× going to robust.

## When to bake off vs run a single profile

**Bake-off is opt-in. Default to a single profile** — pick one from the tables above and run it. Only run a bake-off (N profiles concurrently in worktrees, then pick a winner) if the user specifically asks for one.

Even when asked, push back if any of these are false:

- Three or more profile mixes are genuinely plausible for this work.
- The deliverable is a code diff worth comparing — i.e., you'd be able to tell the arms apart by reading the output.
- Per-arm cost is well under your decision value (rule of thumb: each arm should cost less than the cost of re-running if you guessed wrong).

**Don't bake off:** discovery / scoping / contract-freeze sprints (no diff to compare); short sprints where the bake-off overhead exceeds the work itself; areas where you've already established a profile-task fit on similar prior work.

## How model choice affects outcomes

**The brief is the dominant variable.** All three phase-9 arms in the experiment produced brief-interpretation defects (duplicate file paths, fabricated settled-decisions, brief-violating renames) regardless of profile. Tightening the brief beats picking a better profile. If you only invest in one thing, invest in the brief.

**Where the premium model goes matters more than how many premium models you use.** The single biggest cost-quality win was concentrating the premium model in author-side phases. `marlowe` / `spade-claude` (premium only at plan/revise/gate/review) hit ~3-4× cheaper than `all-claude` and produced higher-quality outputs because the planner read the repo correctly. DeepSeek V4 Pro as the executor is fine — both premium models are overkill there.

**Opus and GPT-5.5 each have role-specific strengths.** Both are good when stakes warrant a premium model:

- **Opus reads existing repo state better as a planner.** Pointed at "implement phase 8" on a repo where phase 8 was already on `main`, Opus-as-planner wrote *"This is already landed at commit X — audit and gap-fill only"* and exited cheaply. Codex-as-planner re-implemented or hit `worker_blocked` from internal sense-check failures. Opus is the safer planner when new work has to fit into existing code.
- **Both are strong critics, in different ways.** Opus surfaces deep, content-distinct flags. Codex is more analytical and catches structural/contract issues; codex-as-critic+gate also steers DeepSeek planners to read the repo before writing. Upgrading the critic from cheap to premium was the single highest-leverage role swap in the experiment — independent of which premium.

**The premium-mono-with-cheap-execution tier.** The `marlowe-*` and `holmes-*` cells (premium-mono column of the cluster grid) put one premium model on *all* reasoning phases while DeepSeek handles mechanical phases. Cheaper than `all-claude`/`all-codex` (which pay premium for execution too) and more expensive than the Kimi-critic column (`spade-*` / `watson-*`). Use when Kimi-as-critic feels light for the stakes but premium execution would be overkill.

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- **"Always use Claude."** Wrong. Codex-as-prep+critic+gate (`nancy`) was a pleasant surprise — it steers DeepSeek planners well and is the cheapest viable profile.
- **"Higher thinking strength always helps."** Wrong. Strength plateaus on sense-check duty; spend it on author-side phases.
- **"Profile choice dominates outcome."** Mostly wrong. Brief quality dominates. If three profiles all produce brief-interpretation defects, fix the brief.

## Inputs that produced these findings

4 implementation phases (orchestrator V1 phases 6-9 in ArtAgents), each with a written brief in `/tmp/phase-N-idea.txt`. ~30 multi-arm bake-offs across 7 distinct profile mixes at light robustness. Per-arm metered cost from session JSONLs. Quality verdicts via blind A/B/C/D sub-agent assessment plus a pre-merge `git diff main --stat` gate.

955	### 16.9 What can be cut under pressure
956	
957	If compressed:
958	
959	- **S6 can shrink to its safety subset** (lint + runbook); defer multi-topic writes. No bot at launch needs them. Saves ~one sprint.
960	- **`set_topic_status` (S4) can slip into S5** if calendar pressure hits.
961	- **S1 and S2a could merge** into one 3-week sprint if the engineer can tolerate it. Not recommended.
962	
963	What is **not** cuttable:
964	
965	- **S2b's `CHECK ... NOT VALID` → VALIDATE → NOT NULL pattern.** Tempting to skip the CHECK step and go straight to NOT NULL; this makes rollback impossible.
966	- **S3 (the join cutover) before any second bot.** Doing it under live multi-bot is dramatically worse than as a no-op.
967	- **S4 solo pre-flight track.** Moving it back into S5 reintroduces the original sizing problem.
968	- **`user_identities` in S1.** Duplicate-human risk (§20.18) is the highest-cost retroactive fix.
969	- **`consult_perspective` clone helper in S4.** Skipping leaves every new `TurnContext` field silently dropped on consult. Single highest correctness defect in the current S4.
970	- **Observability + eval baseline in S2a.** Without them, S3 and S4 cannot detect regressions.
971

974	## 17. Risks
975	
976	- **Scope enforcement is the security model.** Every leak path runs through a tool that didn't consult `ctx.read_scopes`/`ctx.write_scopes`. Centralize the check; add a lint that rejects DB queries in tools that don't pass through the authorization layer.
977	- **`artifact_topics` migration is the largest single migration.** Backfilling memories/observations/themes/watch_items/distillations/OOB rows on a hot DB needs batching and validation queries.

> AGENT

Added §16.10 with per-sprint profile selection. Summary of the picks:

| Sprint | Profile | Robustness | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S1** | `poirot` | `robust` | Apex — permanent schema contract everything downstream depends on |
| **S2a** | `holmes-claude` | `standard` | Cross-cutting hot-path code; Opus reads existing code better |
| **S2b** | `watson-claude` | `standard` | Mechanical SQL flip after soak |
| **S3** | `holmes-claude` | `robust` | Security-shaped audit — every miss = privacy leak |
| **S4** | `poirot` | `standard` | Authorization + `consult_perspective` rewrite; concerns fan out |
| **S5** | `holmes-claude` | `standard` | Net-new code mirroring dyadic shape; pair-review prompt with user |
| **S6** | `watson-claude` | `standard` | Extending established patterns + lint |

The two apex sprints (S1, S4) get `poirot` because they define contracts/security. The two "audit a wide surface" sprints (S2a touching hot path, S3 touching all reads) get `holmes-claude` — Opus-as-planner is the right pick for "find/edit all the existing sites." Mechanical sprints (S2b, S6) drop to `watson-claude` — Kimi-as-critic is enough.

All five reasoning-heavy sprints (S1, S2a, S3, S4, S5) get `--phase-model plan=claude:high`. The skill's asymmetry rule applies — premium planner with cheap critic beats medium-everywhere.

Each sprint also gets a parallel `nancy light` job for runbooks/observability/validation queries (per the "split sprint by work type" rule — don't pay premium for runbook prose).

1	---
2	name: megaplan-model-selection
3	description: Pick the right megaplan profile, thinking-strength tier, and robustness level for the work in front of you — for both Codex and Claude harnesses. Consult before invoking megaplan.
4	---
5	
6	# Profile selection — three questions, three dials
7	
8	Every piece of work answered with three questions. Each question points at one dial. The dials are **independent** — work through each one ignoring the others — then **weigh the three together** holistically to land on a coherent judgment.
9	
10	| | Question | Dial | What it scales | Flag |
11	|---|---|---|---|---|
12	| 1 | What level of raw capability does this need? | **Intelligence tier** | `$/call` | `--profile` |
13	| 2 | What level of process rigor does this need? | **Planning complexity** | `# of calls` | `--robustness` |
14	| 3 | How deeply does each model need to think? | **Depth** | `tokens/call` | `--depth` (with `--phase-model` as the surgical escape hatch) |
15	
16	The dials aren't a mechanical lookup; they're three lenses you apply to the same task, and the answers should fit each other. A high tier with low robustness is usually a mismatch; so is a low tier with `max` depth. When the three feel like they're pulling in opposite directions, the work probably needs to be split.
17	
18	**Defaults to keep in mind:** `--robustness standard`, `--depth` unset (which means the profile's existing depths win — usually `:low` on premium phases), vendor from your config (`claude` if unset). Reach past those only when you can name the specific reason.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Dial 1 — Intelligence tier (5 rungs)
23	
24	> **"What level of raw capability does this need?"**
25	
26	Five tiers, named so the name itself is the proxy. Each rung swaps one block of phases from cheap (DeepSeek / Kimi) to premium (Claude / Codex). The progression is monotonic — once a phase upgrades, it stays upgraded.
27	
28	### When to pick each tier
29	
30	| Tier | Profile | Picks for | Rough cost (light) |
31	|---|---|---|---|
32	| 1 | **`basic`** | Discovery, docs, **and most routine programming**: small features in well-known patterns, schema migrations, ports of self-contained code, utility scripts, config changes, mechanical refactors, CRUD over an existing schema, glue code between known surfaces, test fixtures, anything where the patterns are stable and the number of overlapping concerns is small. Don't underestimate this — it handles a wide range of "I know what to do, just need it written" work. The instinct to reach for tier 3 the moment "code" appears is usually wrong. | ~$0.50-2 |
33	| 2 | **`led`** | Same shape as `basic`, but a premium model writes the plan. Use when the *planning* is the hard part — the implementation is mechanical once mapped out, but you need real thinking to get the map right: complex schema migrations where step ordering matters, multi-step refactors where the sequence needs care, features whose architecture demands deliberation but whose code follows patterns, greenfield implementations with non-trivial design but well-shaped pieces. The cheap models execute confidently once the premium plan exists. Use when you'd say "I just need a smart plan; the rest is following instructions." | ~$1-3 |
34	| 3 | **`thoughtful`** | Novel implementation, cross-cutting code, judgment calls, multi-system features: a new CLI command with cross-cutting concerns, an inbox or routing rewrite, adapters with non-trivial edge cases, plan-mutation verbs touching shared state, export/import surfaces with format edge cases, novel features in a known architecture, refactors with real cross-system implications. Premium handles every reasoning phase (plan, critique, revise, review); DeepSeek handles mechanical phases (prep, gate, finalize, execute). This is the default for *real* engineering work — but only when the work is genuinely novel or cross-cutting. If the patterns are stable and the variables are few, drop back to **`basic`** or **`led`**. | ~$5-15 |
35	| 4 | **`premium`** | Single-vendor premium end-to-end. Use for production-critical work where you want one model's judgment on every phase (including execution) and a clean single-vendor audit trail: schema definitions, wire formats, security-critical code paths, public API contracts, migration logic running against production data, kernel-invariant changes (data structures everything else depends on). Pair with `--robustness robust` for the most complex of these. Pick `--vendor claude` or `--vendor codex` by preference, credits, or prior fit — they're treated as interchangeable. | ~$30-70 |
36	| 5 | **`super-premium`** | Apex — both Claude *and* Codex contributing to the same job. **This is the one tier where the two premium models stop being interchangeable** — Claude and Codex have different strengths (Opus on author/repo-reading side, Codex on critique/structural-analysis side), and the value of this tier comes from combining them. Reach for it when one premium model's depth isn't enough and you want two minds working together: concurrency primitives that cascade (locks, locked event-append, writer epochs, session schemas), schemas all later sprints will build on, wire formats / claim semantics / parent-child propagation rules, multi-system migration decisions, big architectural choices where downstream sprints all depend on what you decide here. Trigger conditions: **(1)** high-stakes — regression = production incident or worse — *or* **(2)** the sprint is *making* a big architectural decision, not just implementing one already made. If neither applies, drop to tier 4. | ~$30-50 |
37	
38	### Which model handles each phase
39	
40	| Phase | basic | led | thoughtful | premium | super-premium |
41	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
42	| **plan**     | DeepSeek | claude   | claude   | claude | claude |
43	| **prep**     | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | claude | claude |
44	| **critique** | Kimi     | Kimi     | claude   | claude | codex  |
45	| **revise**   | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | claude   | claude | claude |
46	| **gate**     | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | claude | claude |
47	| **finalize** | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | claude | claude |
48	| **execute**  | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | DeepSeek | claude | codex  |
49	| **review**   | Kimi     | Kimi     | claude   | claude | codex  |
50	
51	Legend:
52	
53	- **DeepSeek** = DeepSeek V4 Pro (open-source workhorse; competent, structured, cheap).
54	- **Kimi** = Kimi K2 (Fireworks-hosted `kimi-k2p6`; open-source critic; creative, good at spotting issues).
55	- **claude** = Claude Opus 4.7. **codex** = Codex GPT-5.5.
56	
57	**Two things to notice in the phase table:**
58	
59	1. **Each tier adds exactly one block of phases to premium**, and once upgraded, a phase stays upgraded:
60	   - Tier 2 adds `plan` (one phase).
61	   - Tier 3 adds `critique` + `revise` + `review` (the rest of the reasoning loop).
62	   - Tier 4 adds `prep` + `gate` + `finalize` + `execute` (all mechanical and judgment phases).
63	   - Tier 5 doesn't add new premium coverage; it splits the existing premium roles across two vendors.
64	
65	2. **The two open-source models exit in order as you climb.** Kimi exits at tier 3 (sense-check phases get premium). DeepSeek exits at tier 4 (everything else gets premium). At tier 5 the question stops being "premium vs cheap" and becomes "which premium for which role."
66	
67	### Vendor: Claude and Codex are interchangeable at tiers 2-4
68	
69	**Claude and Codex are treated as systematically interchangeable at tiers 2-4 — by policy, not just by observation.** The marginal quality difference between them on a given task is small relative to picking the wrong tier or robustness; encoding per-task vendor preferences would add a dial that doesn't earn its keep. Pick a preferred vendor once (`--vendor`, or `[defaults].vendor` in config) and the preference flows through every tier-2-through-4 profile.
70	
71	**Tier 5 is the exception** — its whole rationale is using both vendors' different strengths together (Opus on author/repo-reading, Codex on critique/structural-analysis). `--vendor` is silently ignored there. The phase table above shows the claude variant for tiers 2-4; for the codex variant, swap `claude`↔`codex` throughout.

74	
75	## Dial 2 — Planning complexity
76	
77	> **"What level of process rigor does this need?"**
78	
79	The `--robustness` flag. Picks how many phases run and how many critique passes happen.
80	
81	| Setting | Workflow | When to use |
82	|---|---|---|
83	| (skip megaplan) | — | Single-file fix, anything you can hold in your head. Just do the work directly. |
84	| `light` | plan → critique → revise → finalize → execute (no prep, no gate, no review) | Small/scoped, well-known feature, low blast radius. ~5 phases instead of 8. |
85	| `standard` *(default)* | prep → plan → critique → gate → revise → finalize → execute → review; 4 critique checks | Cross-cutting, unfamiliar code, ambiguous brief. **Fine for almost everything.** |
86	| `robust` | Same shape as `standard`, 8 critique checks + parallel critique | Security, data migration, public API contract — anything where a regression = production incident. **Extremely rare.** You should be able to name the specific stakes that warrant it. |
87	| `superrobust` | `robust` + parallel review | Both deep critique *and* concurrent review matter. **Vanishingly rare.** Only when the user specifically asks for it. |
88	
89	`standard` is home base. `light` is a cost optimization for cleanly-scoped work. `robust` should feel exceptional — you're saying "this regression would page someone." `superrobust` is a user-requested override, never a default.
90	
91	Cost bands in the tier table above are at `light`. Roughly 1.5-2× the per-phase cost going from `light` → `standard`, and another ~1.3× going to `robust`.
92	
93	---
94	
95	## Dial 3 — Depth
96	
97	> **"How deeply does each model need to think within the tier I picked?"**
98	
99	Picks the thinking strength of the premium model(s) the tier brought in. Independent of tier and robustness — orthogonal lever. Spelled out in the agent spec after a colon (`claude:low`, `codex:medium`, etc.).
100	
101	| Pattern | When to use |
102	|---|---|
103	| `low` planner / `low` critic | **The default.** The pattern is mechanical, intuition is enough, the codebase is well-known. A lot of work lands here even at tier 3 — premium models at `low` thinking are still substantially smarter than the cheap tier, so the upgrade isn't free but doesn't need to be expensive either. |
104	| `medium` planner / `low` critic | Brief is clear but the work has real judgment calls. The plan needs deliberation beyond intuition; the critic still doesn't. |
105	| `high` planner / `low` critic | Brief is long OR codebase is unfamiliar. The planner needs substantial repo-reading and structural reasoning. |
106	| `xhigh` / `max` planner only | Genuinely novel architectural decision. Use sparingly — most "hard" plans don't actually need this. |
107	
108	Available strengths: Claude is `low / medium / high / xhigh / max`; Codex is `minimal / low / medium / high`.
109	
110	**The asymmetry principle:** author phases (plan, revise) can scale all the way up to `max` when the work demands deliberation; sense-check phases (critique, gate, review) plateau at `low` regardless of stakes. A `claude:high` planner + `claude:low` critic is the right shape when the plan needs real thinking — not `claude:medium` everywhere.
111	
112	Default to `low`; only spend on depth when you can name the specific reason the planner needs to deliberate. "Just in case" doesn't earn the cost.
113	
114	---
115	
116	## When to add a prep phase
117	
118	> **"Does the planner need to do explicit research before it can commit to a plan?"**
119	
120	A fourth, narrower lever orthogonal to the three dials. `prep` is a visible research phase that runs *before* `plan` — the planner explicitly reads external docs, surveys an unfamiliar library, maps an API surface, or disambiguates a vague brief. Off by default (most work doesn't need a discovery step; adding one without need just costs tokens and wall-clock). Enable with `--with-prep`.
121	
122	**Reach for it when at least one of these is true:**
123	
124	- **External APIs whose semantics aren't already known** — the planner has to read API docs before deciding what calls to make.
125	- **Unfamiliar libraries or frameworks** — codebase patterns aren't enough; the planner needs to survey the library's API surface first.
126	- **Research-heavy briefs** — the work is research-bounded ("figure out how X behaves, then implement").
127	- **Ambiguous or under-specified requirements** — the planner needs a budget to disambiguate explicitly instead of interleaving with planning.
128	- **Integration work where target-system behavior must be discovered** — wire formats, error semantics, performance characteristics undocumented in the codebase.
129	
130	If none apply, leave the flag off. "Prep just in case" doesn't earn its cost. Redundant at `robust` and `superrobust` (those already include prep); the flag's value is at `light` and `standard`, where prep is normally skipped.
131	
132	---
133	
134	## Notation for recording profile choices
135	
136	For sprint notes, brief headers, commit messages, or anywhere you need to write down a profile choice compactly, use the slash form: **`profile/robustness/depth`** — defaults can be omitted.
137	
138	Order is fixed left-to-right: tier → robustness → depth, matching dial numbers 1 → 2 → 3. The `//` reads as "skip the middle slot — defaults there."
139	
140	### Spine examples (just the three dials)
141

144	| Tier-1 work at default robustness and depth | `basic` |
145	| Tier-1 work at light robustness | `basic/light` |
146	| Tier-2 work at defaults | `led` |
147	| Tier-3 work at defaults | `thoughtful` |
148	| Tier-3 work with depth bumped to high (default robustness) | `thoughtful//high` |
149	| Tier-3 work with medium depth (default robustness) | `thoughtful//medium` |
150	| Tier-4 work at robust + high depth | `premium/robust/high` |

154	
155	For `--vendor`, `--critic`, `--with-prep`, append modifiers without disturbing the spine. The conventions:
156	
157	- `@<vendor>` — vendor override (e.g. `@codex`).
158	- `, critic=<kind>` — critic override (e.g. `, critic=kimi`).
159	- `+prep` — enable the prep phase.

163	| Tier-2 work, prefer codex | `led @codex` |

171	
172	The shorthand is for **recording**, not for the CLI. Use it in:
173	
174	- Sprint planning docs ("Sprint 14 — `thoughtful//high +prep`")
175	- Brief headers (`[premium/robust/high]` as the first line of a brief)
176	- Commit messages ("ran as `thoughtful`, defaults")
177	- Slack / chat references when describing a sprint setup at a glance
178	
179	The actual invocation is still `megaplan init --profile … --robustness … --depth …` — see "Running it" below for the mapping.
180	
181	---
182	
183	## Running it — profile plus the knobs
184	
185	The invocation has three layers: three flags for the dials, three modifiers for orthogonal toggles, one escape hatch for surgical needs.
186	
187	### The three dial flags
188	
189	1. **`--profile`** — the tier name (`basic`, `led`, `thoughtful`, `premium`, `super-premium`).
190	2. **`--robustness light|standard|robust|superrobust`** — `standard` is home base.
191	3. **`--depth low|medium|high|xhigh|max`** — rewrites the effort suffix on author-side claude/codex slots (plan, revise, loop_plan, tiebreaker_*) at the resolved vendor. Critic + mechanical phases plateau at their existing depth (the asymmetry principle). Defaults to whatever the profile sets (usually `:low`). Honored on vendor-locked profiles. Codex caps at `high`; Claude adds `xhigh` and `max`.
192	
193	### The three modifier flags
194	
195	- **`--vendor claude|codex`** — vendor override at tiers 2-4. Defaults to `[defaults].vendor` in `~/.config/megaplan/config.toml` (or `claude` if unset). Tier 1 ignores it (no premium phases); tier 5 silently ignores it (vendor-locked).
196	- **`--critic kimi|cross`** — overrides the critique+review pair (preserving the invariant — see below). `kimi` swaps in Kimi for both phases; `cross` swaps to the other premium vendor relative to `--vendor`. Silently ignored at tier 5.
197	- **`--with-prep`** — force the `prep` research phase into the workflow regardless of `--robustness`. Off by default; no-op at `robust`/`superrobust`. See "When to add a prep phase" above.
198	
199	### The escape hatch
200	
201	**`--phase-model phase=spec`**, repeatable. For when `--depth` is too coarse — e.g. bump just `critique` without touching the rest. Most runs don't need it.
202	
203	### Where the flags live
204	
205	`--vendor`, `--depth`, and `--critic` are wired on every subcommand that accepts `--profile`:
206	
207	- `megaplan init`
208	- the step parsers (`prep`, `plan`, `critique`, `gate`, `revise`, `finalize`, `execute`, `review`, etc.)
209	- `megaplan loop init`, `megaplan loop run`
210	- `megaplan tiebreaker run` and the bare `megaplan tiebreaker` default-run action
211	
212	The flags default to `None`, which means "consult the config default" — only override when you specifically want the other premium or a non-default critic.
213	
214	### Mid-flight overrides
215	
216	For when the work turns out different than expected:
217	
218	- `megaplan override set-profile --profile NAME --plan ID` — swap tier mid-run. Started on `thoughtful`, hit something gnarlier, escalate to `premium` for the remainder.
219	- `megaplan override set-robustness --robustness LEVEL --plan ID` — same for the planning-complexity dial.
220	- `megaplan override replan --plan ID` — back up to planning and redo with whatever models / robustness are now active.
221	
222	Lean on these instead of inventing new profile names. If you find yourself thinking "I want a profile that's *like* `thoughtful` but with X" — the answer is almost always `thoughtful` plus an override, not a new profile.
223	
224	### The critique == review invariant
225	
226	The model that critiques the plan also reviews the executed work — same mind pre-execution and post-execution. Wiring them to the same non-author model gives you one coherent second mind across both checkpoints instead of two disjointed ones, and keeps the author's blindspots out of the sense-check loop. Every built-in tier honors this.
227	
228	`--critic` bundles the two phases in one flag and preserves the invariant. Bare `--phase-model` does not — if you override critique with `--phase-model`, override review the same way, or use `--critic` instead.
229	
230	### Worked invocations
231	
232	> *"Schema migration where step ordering is intricate but each step is mechanical. Prefer codex; brief is clear so default depth is fine."*
233	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile led --vendor codex`
234	
235	> *"Novel feature, cross-cutting, brief is long, codebase is unfamiliar."*
236	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile thoughtful --depth high` *(vendor defaults from config; depth lifts plan + revise + loop_plan + tiebreaker_* to claude:high; critic + mechanical stay at their defaults)*
237	
238	> *"Novel feature involving an external API we haven't used before. Planner needs to read the API docs before committing."*
239	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile thoughtful --with-prep --depth medium` *(adds the visible `prep` phase even at `standard` robustness, so the planner can survey the API surface before producing a plan)*
240	
241	> *"Cross-cutting feature, tier 3, but I want Kimi catching what the premium author missed (legacy `spade-claude` behaviour)."*
242	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile thoughtful --critic kimi`
243	
244	> *"Migration logic against production data. I want kimi critiquing this even though it's tier 4."*
245	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile premium --robustness robust --depth high --critic kimi`
246	
247	> *"Schema everyone downstream will build on. Apex tier."*
248	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile super-premium --robustness robust --depth high`
249	
250	> *"Tier-3 work, brief is clear, but I want the critic to deliberate a little more — the planner can stay at the profile default."*
251	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile thoughtful --phase-model critique=claude:medium --phase-model review=claude:medium` *(surgical: bump just one pair, leave plan + revise at the profile's `:low`. The kind of override `--depth` can't express because it's by-phase-name, not by-author-vs-critic.)*
252	
253	> *"Verification sprint, mostly text, lowest-stakes thing in the queue."*
254	> `megaplan init <brief> --profile basic --robustness light`
255	
256	Three pieces of intent → three flags (`--profile`, `--robustness`, `--depth`), plus `--vendor` / `--critic` / `--with-prep` when you need them.
257	
258	---
259	
260	## The canonical catalog
261	
262	Five tier names + two flags cover the whole rubric. A handful of legacy aliases are preserved for back-compat.
263	
264	### Canonical (use these)
265	
266	| Profile | Tier | Where it sits |
267	|---|---|---|
268	| `basic` | 1 | All cheap; Kimi critiques+reviews. |
269	| `led` | 2 | Premium plan only; everything else cheap. |
270	| `thoughtful` | 3 | Premium reasoning loop; DeepSeek mechanical. The default for real engineering. |
271	| `premium` | 4 | Single-vendor premium end-to-end at `:low` depth. Pick the vendor with `--vendor`. |
272	| `super-premium` | 5 | Vendor-locked Claude/Codex split. The apex; `--vendor` and `--critic` are silently ignored. |
273	
274	Vendor, depth, and critic flavor are flags on these, not separate profiles: `--vendor claude|codex` at tiers 2-4, `--depth low|medium|high|xhigh|max` to set author-phase thinking depth, `--critic kimi|cross` to override the critique+review pair.
275	
276	### Legacy aliases (still loaded; modern equivalent listed)
277	
278	| Profile | What it is | Modern equivalent |
279	|---|---|---|
280	| `nancy` | Nancy Drew — DeepSeek lead + executor, `codex:medium` prep/critique/gate/review. Cheapest profile with a premium critic. | Closest is `led --critic cross` (Codex critic over a Claude/Codex-planned base), but the recipe doesn't have a 1:1 mapping. Keep using `nancy` if scripts rely on it. |
281	| `marlowe` | Legacy `claude:low` author with Kimi critic + Claude-on-review. Predates the `critique == review` invariant. | `thoughtful --critic kimi` is the spiritual successor, but it routes review through Kimi (honoring the invariant) instead of Claude. Use `marlowe` if you specifically want Claude doing the post-execute review. |
282	| `holmes` | Legacy medium-effort with a cross-model gate (`codex:medium` gate/review alongside `claude:medium` plan/revise). | No exact match — the rubric doesn't carve out cross-model gate behaviour. Closest is `thoughtful --critic cross --phase-model plan=claude:medium --phase-model revise=claude:medium`. Keep using `holmes` if cross-model gate is the point. |
283	| `marlowe-claude` / `marlowe-codex` | Low-effort cluster: claude (or codex) author, *other* premium critic. | `thoughtful --critic cross` (`--vendor claude` or `codex` picks the author). |
284	| `spade-claude` / `spade-codex` | Low-effort cluster: claude (or codex) author, Kimi critic. | `thoughtful --critic kimi --vendor claude\|codex`. |
285	| `holmes-claude` / `holmes-codex` | Medium-effort cluster: claude (or codex) author at `:medium`, other premium critic. | `thoughtful --critic cross --vendor … --phase-model plan=claude:medium --phase-model revise=claude:medium`. |
286	| `watson-claude` / `watson-codex` | Medium-effort cluster: claude (or codex) author at `:medium`, Kimi critic. | `thoughtful --critic kimi --vendor … --phase-model plan=claude:medium --phase-model revise=claude:medium`. |
287	| `all-claude` / `all-codex` | Single vendor at default effort (no `:low` suffix) for every phase. | `premium --vendor claude\|codex`, **but the depths differ** — see `premium ≠ all-claude` in migration notes. |
288	| `poirot` | Hercule Poirot — vendor-locked Claude+Codex split at default effort. Mirrors `super-premium`. | `super-premium`. Both are vendor-locked and use the same phase map. Pick either; keep `poirot` for personality / legacy scripts. |
289	| `standard` | Same shape as `poirot` / `super-premium` but lives in the megaplan core as the built-in fallback. | `super-premium`. |
290	| `all-deepseek-pro` / `all-deepseek-flash` / `all-fireworks-deepseek` | DeepSeek end-to-end (different deployments). | Use directly when you specifically want DeepSeek-only — they're below tier 1 on the rubric ladder. |
291	| `all-open` | Kimi author + GLM-5.1 critic/executor. Fully-open analogue of `super-premium`. | Use directly when you want open-source apex; no rubric-tier equivalent. |
292	
293	### Project- and user-level overrides
294	
295	Built-in profiles live in `megaplan/profiles/` and ship with the package. To customize:
296	
297	- Per-user: `~/.config/megaplan/profiles.toml`.
298	- Per-project: `<project>/.megaplan/profiles.toml`.
299	
300	Project overrides win over user overrides win over built-ins. The TOML schema is `[profiles.<name>]` with one key per phase (plus optional `vendor_locked = true`).
301	
302	---
303	
304	## Config defaults
305	
306	The `--vendor` flag honors a per-user config default. Write `~/.config/megaplan/config.toml`:
307	
308	```toml
309	[defaults]
310	vendor = "claude"   # "claude" or "codex"
311	```
312	
313	Set this once on a new machine and tiers 2-4 default to your preferred premium without per-invocation flags. The CLI flag still wins when passed.
314	
315	A malformed or missing config falls back to `claude` silently — the loader fails open.
316	
317	---
318	
319	## Migration notes
320	
321	The rubric's canonical catalog supersedes the old detective grid. Existing scripts keep working (every legacy name still resolves), but a few sharp edges are worth flagging.
322	
323	### `super-premium` and `poirot` are vendor-locked
324	
325	Both profiles set `vendor_locked = true`. `--vendor` and `--critic` are silently ignored on vendor-locked profiles — the locked profile's existing model assignments win, with no error or warning. Their whole rationale is using Claude and Codex together, so collapsing to a single vendor or swapping the critic would change the tier's identity, not its tuning, and the loader treats those flags as no-ops rather than failures.
326	
327	`--depth` **is honored** on vendor-locked profiles (depth is about how hard each model thinks, not which vendor is filling the slot). `--phase-model` also still works as the surgical escape hatch when you need finer control than `--depth` can give.
328	
329	### `premium` ≠ `all-claude`
330	
331	This is the trap. `all-claude` uses bare `claude` for every phase, which means **default effort** in the agent spec parser. `premium --vendor claude` uses `claude:low` for every phase. The two are not interchangeable on cost or output — `:low` is meaningfully cheaper and shallower than default effort.
332	
333	- **Scripts pinned to `all-claude` / `all-codex`** keep their existing behaviour. No change required.
334	- **Users picking the rubric default at tier 4** should reach for `--profile premium` and (if needed) bump depth explicitly via `--depth high` (or `--phase-model plan=claude:high` for surgical control). That matches the rubric's "premium at `:low` is the right floor" principle.
335	
336	### `--critic cross` at tier 1 is a footgun
337	
338	The flag accepts the combination, but it doesn't make rubric sense — there's no premium *author* for the cross-vendor critic to be cross-vendor *to*. The tier-1 profile has no premium model at all; "cross of nothing" is undefined.
339	
340	If you want a premium critic at tier 1, step up to `led --critic cross` (which actually has a premium author to be cross-vendor relative to) or `thoughtful --critic kimi` (the closest cheap-pipeline-with-premium-critique shape).
341	
342	### Legacy detective-cluster scripts
343	
344	Scripts using `marlowe-*`, `spade-*`, `holmes-*`, `watson-*` keep working — the profiles ship unchanged. There's no rush to migrate. New work should prefer `thoughtful` plus `--vendor` / `--critic` / `--phase-model`; the legacy names are kept because they have known cost/quality data from prior runs.
345	
346	### Kimi spec migrated to Fireworks `kimi-k2p6`
347	
348	The canonical Kimi spec changed from `hermes:moonshotai/kimi-k2.6` (OpenRouter-routed) to `hermes:fireworks:accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k2p6` (Fireworks-direct). Every built-in profile that used Kimi (`basic`, `led`, `marlowe`, `holmes`, the `spade-*` / `watson-*` clusters, `all-open`) has been updated; `--critic kimi` now writes the new spec via `KIMI_SPEC`.
349	
350	- **Scripts that don't pin the spec** keep working without changes — the rewrite is internal.
351	- **Scripts that pin the old spec via `--phase-model critique=hermes:moonshotai/kimi-k2.6`** still parse and run *as strings*, but they'll be calling a model that may no longer be available on OpenRouter. Replace the pinned spec with `hermes:fireworks:accounts/fireworks/models/kimi-k2p6`, or — usually cleaner — drop the `--phase-model` pin in favor of `--critic kimi`, which always tracks the canonical Kimi spec.
352	
353	### DeepSeek spec migrated to Fireworks `deepseek-v4-pro`
354	
355	The canonical DeepSeek spec changed from `hermes:deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro` (DeepSeek's direct API via OpenRouter) and `hermes:deepseek:deepseek-v4-pro` (direct-provider form) to `hermes:fireworks:accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v4-pro` (Fireworks-direct). Every built-in profile that used DeepSeek (`basic`, `led`, `thoughtful`, `marlowe`, `holmes`, `nancy`, the detective cluster, `all-deepseek-pro`) has been updated.
356	
357	- **Scripts that don't pin the spec** keep working without changes — the rewrite is internal.
358	- **Scripts that pin the old spec via `--phase-model`** still parse and run *as strings*; they'll route via the previous provider as long as those routes remain configured. Migrate the pinned spec to `hermes:fireworks:accounts/fireworks/models/deepseek-v4-pro` to match the new canonical routing.
359

380	---
381	
382	## Operating principles
383	
384	A few load-bearing reminders that the rubric is built on.
385	
386	**The brief is the dominant variable.** Brief-interpretation defects (duplicate paths, fabricated decisions, brief-violating renames) show up across every profile. Tightening the brief beats picking a better profile. If you only invest in one thing, invest in the brief.
387	
388	**Where the premium model goes matters more than how many premium models you use.** Concentrating the premium model in author-side phases (plan, revise) gives the biggest cost-quality win. DeepSeek as the executor is fine — premium there is overkill. This is why tiers 1-3 spend nothing on premium execution.
389	
390	**Size each megaplan to ~2 weeks max.** A megaplan should fit a sprint — roughly two weeks of work, give or take. Larger scopes don't survive the brief-to-execution distance; the plan drifts, the critique loses focus, the review can't hold the whole shape in one pass. If you're scoping work that genuinely needs a month, split it into 2–3 sprints with explicit handoffs (each its own brief, its own profile, its own retro). The two-week ceiling isn't about calendar time so much as about how much *one coherent plan* can carry.
391	
392	**One profile per sprint.** Within that ~2-week window, pick the profile that matches the **highest-stakes deliverable** in the sprint; lower-stakes items inherit the tier. Operational simplicity beats the savings from splitting. Only split when the lower-stakes work is *substantial* (multiple days) **and** independent. Structure the plan so cheap work lives in cheap sprints, not interleaved inside expensive ones.
393	
394	**Bake-off is opt-in.** Default to a single profile. Only run a multi-arm bake-off when (a) the user asks, (b) three or more mixes are genuinely plausible, (c) the deliverable is a diff worth comparing, and (d) per-arm cost is well below the cost of guessing wrong. Don't bake off discovery / scoping / contract-freeze sprints — no diff to compare.
395	
396	**Anti-patterns:**
397	
398	- *"Always use Claude."* Wrong. Codex on prep/critique/gate steers DeepSeek planners well and is the cheapest viable premium-critic profile.
399	- *"Higher thinking strength always helps."* Wrong. Strength plateaus on sense-check duty; spend it on author-side phases only.
400	- *"Profile choice dominates outcome."* Mostly wrong. Brief quality dominates. If three profiles all produce brief-interpretation defects, fix the brief.
401	
402	### Calibration caveats
403	
404	A couple of places where the rubric is more confident-sounding than the evidence warrants:
405	
406	- **Tier 2 (`led`) is a design point, not a measured one.** "Premium plan only, everything else cheap" is theoretically clean (concentrate spend where it pays off most) but hasn't been bake-off validated against tier 1 or tier 3 on intermediate-complexity work. Reach for it when the shape fits, but treat it as a hypothesis until we have runs to compare. If `led` consistently underperforms `thoughtful` on real work, the right answer may be to drop it and accept that there's no intermediate tier.
407	- **Cost bands for tiers 1-2 are projections, not runs.** Tiers 3-5 have prior-run data behind their numbers; tiers 1-2 are estimates based on the model mix. Expect them to shift once we have real invocations to measure against.
408

> AGENT

Rewrote §16.10 against the current rubric. The detective grid is now legacy aliases; the canonical setup is **three independent dials**: profile tier (`basic` → `super-premium`), robustness (`light`/`standard`/`robust`), and depth (`low` → `max`).

**The mapping shift was substantial:**

| Sprint | Old (deprecated) | New (canonical) |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | `poirot robust` + plan/revise high | `super-premium/robust/high` |
| S2a | `holmes-claude standard` + plan/revise high | `thoughtful//high` |
| S2b | `marlowe-claude standard` | `led` |
| S3 | `holmes-claude robust` + plan/revise high | `premium/robust/high, critic=cross` |
| S4 | `poirot standard` + plan/revise high | `super-premium//high` |
| S5 | `holmes-claude standard` + plan/revise high | `thoughtful//high` |
| S6 | `spade-claude light` | `basic/light` |

**What changed structurally beyond the renaming:**

- **S2b → `led`** is the cleanest fit. The new rubric specifically describes `led` as "complex schema migrations where step ordering matters" — exactly S2b. Premium plan, cheap execution. The old "marlowe-claude" framing was awkward; `led` is the intended shape.
- **S3 → `premium/robust/high, critic=cross`** rather than apex. The new rubric distinguishes "implementing a security-critical decision" (tier 4) from "making a security-critical architectural decision" (tier 5). S3 implements the S1 decision. `--critic cross` gets the second-vendor mind on the audit at substantially lower cost than `super-premium`.
- **`high` depth as the default for author-side phases** when the brief is long — applied uniformly to S1/S2a/S3/S4/S5. The `--depth` flag handles this cleanly without per-phase overrides.
- **No `--with-prep` anywhere** — the rubric's prep criteria (external APIs, unfamiliar libraries, research briefs) don't fit any sprint in this plan.
- **Dropped the per-sprint nancy fan-out.** The new rubric explicitly says: "Operational simplicity beats the savings from splitting. Only split when lower-stakes work is *substantial* (multiple days) **and** independent." None of the runbooks/dashboards qualify.

Vendor preference (claude over codex on S2a/S3/S5) now lives in `~/.config/megaplan/config.toml` as `vendor = "claude"`, not per-sprint flags — the new rubric treats them as interchangeable at tiers 2–4 by policy.

1020	## 17. Risks
1021	
1022	- **Scope enforcement is the security model.** Every leak path runs through a tool that didn't consult `ctx.read_scopes`/`ctx.write_scopes`. Centralize the check; add a lint that rejects DB queries in tools that don't pass through the authorization layer.
1023	- **`artifact_topics` migration is the largest single migration.** Backfilling memories/observations/themes/watch_items/distillations/OOB rows on a hot DB needs batching and validation queries.
1024	- **OOB nullable membership semantics.** Global OOB is "no row in `artifact_topics`." Make this loud in code review.
1025	- **Newer-inbound suppression cutover.** Re-keying mid-deploy will briefly let stale sends through. Drain or use a feature flag.
1026	- **Channel routing is security-sensitive.** Startup integrity check: every channel resolves to a known bot; FK with `ON DELETE RESTRICT`.
1027	- **Prompt token budget.** Status + peek compound with topic count. Cap peek to N most-recently-active topics; enforce headline ≤ 80 chars, body ≤ 300; cap injected statuses.

# Megaplan profile recommendations for the 7-sprint multi-agent architecture plan

## 1. Per-sprint table

| # | Sprint | Pick | One-line rationale |

| S1 | Foundation schema + code shape | `led//medium` | Six additive migrations + dataclass plumbing — design is locked in §3–§12; the planner needs to sequence migrations and backfill cursors carefully, but execution is mechanical. |

| S3 | `artifact_topics` join cutover for reads | `thoughtful//high` | A full data-access audit across 7 files with the sleeper-bug-shaped `decay.py` judgment call; long brief, partly unfamiliar repo surface, behavior must be byte-identical. |
| S4 | Authorization + topic status + solo pre-flight | `premium/robust/high` | Scope enforcement is the security model (§17); a regression here is a data-leak production incident — the rubric's specifically-named `robust` trigger. |
| S5 | First solo bot (code) | `thoughtful//medium` | Novel implementation of solo renderer/hot-context/crisis files in a now-known architecture, with real judgment about what dyadic logic to strip. |
| S6 | Multi-topic writes + hardening | `led` | Mechanism-only extensions of patterns already established in S1–S5; design is documented in §8.2, no active bot exercises it at launch. |

## 2. Rationale per sprint

### S1 — `led//medium`

**Tier.** The architectural decisions are *already made* in §3–§12; this sprint *implements* them as additive migrations and optional dataclass fields. That matches the rubric's tier-2 description almost verbatim: "complex schema migrations where step ordering matters … features whose architecture demands deliberation but whose code follows patterns." It's not tier 3 because no novel design is being created — the brief is a documented blueprint to execute. The instinct-trap warning in the tier-1 row ("the instinct to reach for tier 3 the moment 'code' appears is usually wrong") applies one rung up too: there's no genuine *cross-system judgment* here that the cheap executor can't follow once the migration order and backfill rule are pinned down.

**Robustness.** `standard`. The work is additive and nullable — S2b applies NOT NULL only after a 7-day soak. A backfill bug surfaces as orphaned `artifact_topics` rows discoverable by the named validation queries, not as a production outage. Not `robust`: the rubric reserves that for "regression = production incident," and additive migrations with named rollback don't clear that bar.

**Depth.** `medium` planner. The brief is long (6 migrations, 4 code modules, cursor-keyed resumable backfill, an OOB classification rule that resolves a documented §19/§20 ambiguity, a CHECK constraint typo the doc explicitly flags). The planner needs deliberation beyond intuition to sequence this; the critic and executor don't.

**Prep / vendor / critic.** None. Codebase is the team's own; no external APIs.

### S2a — `thoughtful//medium`

**Tier.** Tier 3 lands cleanly. The brief is an *inbox/routing rewrite* shape — the rubric names this explicitly. Cross-cutting work spanning `inbound.py`, `messaging.py`, `agentic.py:483/577/612`, `scheduled_jobs.py:216`, `write_tools.py:1367`, every artifact write, plus a dual-key transition with non-trivial semantics (`bot_id = ctx.bot_id OR bot_id IS NULL` during the transition window). Real judgment calls in the planner: where the transaction boundary goes for artifact+`artifact_topics`, how the dual-key coalescer flushes on deploy, what the lint regex looks like. Tier 2 isn't enough because the planner alone can't carry this — the critic needs to catch missed insert sites.

**Robustness.** `standard`. Cross-cutting and ambiguous-brief-shaped ("find every insert site, broader than the obvious ones") but the doc names the soak gate in S2b as the safety net. Not `robust`: no individual stamping miss is a production incident; it becomes one only at S2b NOT NULL, and the soak window catches it.

**Depth.** `medium`. The brief is long; the dual-key transition needs deliberation. Not `high` — the touched files are well-known mediator code, no deep repo-reading needed.

### S2b — `led`

**Tier.** This is the rubric's tier-2 archetype: "complex schema migrations where step ordering matters." The five-step `CHECK NOT VALID → VALIDATE → NOT NULL → drop CHECK → retire legacy paths` recipe is well-established Postgres practice. Once the plan names the precondition (S2a soak with zero NULLs in the active window) and the sequence, the SQL is mechanical. Reach-for-tier-3 instinct should resist here.

**Robustness.** `standard`. The recipe itself is the rollback safety; the doc says "rollback target locked." A NOT NULL apply that finds a straggling row fails loudly, doesn't corrupt anything.

**Depth.** Default `low`. The brief is short, the patterns are explicit, and the doc's §16.9 specifically calls out this pattern as non-cuttable, meaning it's well-shaped enough to deserve precision but not deep judgment.

### S3 — `thoughtful//high`

**Tier.** "Full data-access audit sprint" with a sleeper bug specifically called out in `decay.py` (today's decay walks themes/observations/watch items globally — picking per-topic vs global is a *real* design call this sprint must close). 50+ query sites across `hot_context.py`, `read_tools.py`, `oob_check.py`, `cross_thread_privacy.py`, `scheduled_job_handlers.py`, `decay.py`, `withheld_reviews.py`. Not tier 4 because the design decision (route every read through the join) is already made; this is exhaustive implementation against an existing architecture.

**Robustness.** `standard`. I considered `robust` because a missed read site = future data leak when bots #2+ exist, but the lint added in this sprint plus S4's authorization layer are the real safety nets. The blast radius this sprint is bounded — mediator is still the only consumer, so a missed read site shows up as an EXPLAIN regression or a frozen-fixture diff, not an incident.

**Depth.** `high` planner. The brief is long *and* the codebase surface is partly unfamiliar (`decay.py`, `withheld_reviews.py`, `cross_thread_privacy.py` aren't core mediator paths). ### S4 — `premium/robust/high`

**Tier.** Tier 4. This is the sprint that ships the security model. §17 lead bullet: "Scope enforcement is the security model. Every leak path runs through a tool that didn't consult `ctx.read_scopes`/`ctx.write_scopes`." The rubric's tier-4 trigger names this almost exactly: "production-critical work where you want one model's judgment on every phase (including execution) and a clean single-vendor audit trail: …security-critical code paths, public API contracts…" Three concrete tier-4 markers: (a) authorization layer with negative-permission CI tests, (b) `consult_perspective` clone helper named in §16.9 as the *single highest correctness defect* if skipped, (c) tool-schema changes on 19 tools that are explicit "model-behavior risk."
